text: {"boxes":[{"excerpt":"The IMF’s data on the currency composition of foreign exchange (FX) reserves is scrutinized carefully for any signs that the world is shifting way from the dollar.","claim":"Does the IMF's data on the currency composition of central bank reserves actually tell us whether the world is moving away from the dollar?","role":"question","explicit":false,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[2,3],"reason":"A widely watched indicator should be judged by how much of the underlying activity it actually captures."},{"excerpt":"Yet it doesn’t really matter that much if the dollar’s share of reserves has shifted from 56.5 percent to 57 percent. The ink-to-impact ratio of the quarterly reporting on the latest COFER data is all off.","claim":"Analysts who focus on small quarterly shifts in the dollar's COFER reserve share are watching the wrong indicator.","role":"opposing_view","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[2,3,13,41],"reason":"Small changes in a stagnant stock say little about where new flows are going."},{"excerpt":"Neither the stock of global reserves nor the stock of dollar reserves has changed much in the last ten years.","claim":"Global reserves and dollar reserves have both been roughly flat for a decade.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[4,25,30],"reason":"A flat stock cannot be the source of significant new demand for an asset."},{"excerpt":"China’s state banks (per the Bank of International Settlements) have almost as many foreign assets as the central bank (PBOC).","claim":"In China, Japan, Korea and Saudi Arabia, state banks, pension funds or sovereign funds hold foreign assets comparable to or larger than the central bank's or government's reserves.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[6,7,8,11,36],"reason":"Official foreign assets held outside the central bank are still sovereign wealth and belong in the count."},{"excerpt":"Asia’s big surplus economies are in a sense just catching up with the world’s oil exporters.","claim":"Asian surplus economies are following oil exporters in channelling surpluses into sovereign funds and other non-reserve public vehicles.","role":"intermediate_claim","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[11],"reason":"Surplus countries tend to move accumulated savings from low-yield reserves into higher-return state investors as their holdings grow."},{"excerpt":"China reports $3.3 trillion in gross foreign assets to the BIS","claim":"China's state banks hold about $3.3 trillion in gross foreign assets, matching about $4 trillion in banking outflows in the balance of payments; the top five banks report $2.5 trillion in foreign currency assets; AidData points to nearly $1 trillion at the policy banks; and since 2010 net bank outflows have exceeded reserve accumulation.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[15,16,17,18,19],"reason":"An estimate gains confidence when independent data sources point to the same order of magnitude."},{"excerpt":"The Chinese haven’t disclosed the foreign assets of the two policy banks (with at this stage the complicity of the IMF, which has neither analyzed the role of SAFE policy bank financing, nor highlighted the glaring gap in China’s own reporting).","claim":"China's official reporting is incomplete and the IMF has failed to flag the gap, so reported data understate sovereign foreign assets.","role":"source_credibility","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[19],"reason":"A gap left by the reporter and ignored by its overseer should push analysts toward independent sources."},{"excerpt":"SAFE’s disclosure—which covers the commercial banks—puts the dollar share of their offshore foreign currency assets at around 70 percent.","claim":"About 70 percent of Chinese state banks' foreign currency assets are in dollars, above the 55 percent last disclosed for formal reserves.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[20,21,38],"reason":"Comparing the currency mix of two pools shows which one is more dollar-heavy."},{"excerpt":"Put simply, SAFE’s static dollar holdings aren’t the important story.","claim":"In China the important story is the rapid growth of the state banks' dollar holdings, not SAFE's static reserves.","role":"intermediate_claim","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[22,23],"reason":"The growing pool, not the static one, drives marginal demand."},{"excerpt":"What has grown is the foreign portfolio of the GPIF. it was around $400 billion in 2014, ~$1 trillion in Q1 of 2026.","claim":"Japan's reserves stayed near $1.1-1.2 trillion as intervention offset interest income, while GPIF's foreign portfolio grew from about $400 billion to about $1 trillion, with about half of its foreign bonds and 65 percent of its foreign equities in U.S. assets.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[24,25,26,27,28],"reason":"Growth in a public pension fund's foreign portfolio adds to state foreign assets even when reserves are flat."},{"excerpt":"From 2012 to 2025, the foreign assets at the NPS have grown from ~$80 billion (around 21 percent of total assets) to over $660 billion (55 percent of total assets)—and something like 70 percent of those are in dollars.","claim":"Korea's NPS foreign assets rose from $80 billion to over $660 billion, about 70 percent in dollars, while Bank of Korea reserves stayed around $375-450 billion.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[29,30,31],"reason":"A state fund that outgrows the central bank becomes the main official holder of foreign currency."},{"excerpt":"the majority of the dollar assets held by Korea’s government (the NPS reports to the Ministry of Health and Welfare, and the Minister of Health chairs its asset allocation committee) aren’t held by the central bank and aren’t in the IMF’s COFER data set.","claim":"Most of Korea's government dollar assets sit outside the central bank and outside COFER.","role":"intermediate_claim","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[32],"reason":"Government control, not the legal form of the holder, determines whether assets are effectively sovereign."},{"excerpt":"Taiwan is an unusual case, as the life insurers aren’t technically sovereign investors.","claim":"Taiwan's life insurers have taken on a quasi-official role because the regulator sets their hedge ratios and the central bank uses them to manage the currency; they hold over 95 percent of foreign assets in dollars.","role":"case_type","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[9,10,33],"reason":"Private institutions whose positions the state directs and whose solvency it backs function as quasi-sovereign investors."},{"excerpt":"So too does the PBOC’s use of the “macroprudential adjustment factor” effectively adjust banks’ net foreign assets","claim":"Authorities manage their currencies by adjusting the foreign positions of state-influenced banks and insurers, which moves foreign asset accumulation off the central bank's balance sheet.","role":"mechanism","explicit":true,"kind":"economic","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[9,10,33],"reason":"Regulatory levers over intermediaries' foreign exposure can stand in for direct reserve intervention."},{"excerpt":"It keeps roughly $200 billion of its $250 billion in foreign investments in dollars—well above the U.S. share of a standard global stock index.","claim":"Saudi Arabia's PIF holds about $200 billion of its $250 billion in foreign assets in dollars, and its foreign assets are close in size to SAMA's reserves.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[34,35,36],"reason":"A dollar share above the global index weight indicates a deliberate tilt toward the dollar."},{"excerpt":"the available evidence suggests that the dollar share of these pools is in line with or higher than the dollar share of global FX reserves","claim":"The dollar share of these quasi-sovereign pools generally equals or exceeds the dollar share of formal reserves.","role":"intermediate_claim","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[12,38,44],"reason":"Judging dollar demand by reserves alone is biased if uncounted pools are more dollar-heavy."},{"excerpt":"Japan is the main exception; the GPIF’s dollar share is below the likely dollar share of Japan’s MoF.","claim":"Japan is the exception, since GPIF's dollar share is likely below that of the Ministry of Finance's reserves, and the dollar tilt holds only 'for now'.","role":"caveat","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[44,51,12],"reason":"A general pattern should acknowledge its known exceptions and that it may not last."},{"excerpt":"The broad story is thus pretty clear: the growth in the world’s sovereign and quasi-sovereign assets is not coming through an increase in FX reserve holdings managed by the world’s central banks.","claim":"The story is de-reservification rather than de-dollarization: sovereign foreign asset growth has moved from central bank reserves to quasi-sovereign investors that remain heavily dollar-weighted, so the dollar's reserve role is not a source of new inflows and COFER misses the action.","role":"main_claim","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"single","paragraphs":[13,37,41,42,43],"reason":"An asset's international role depends on all sovereign and quasi-sovereign portfolio choices, not only the narrowest official category."},{"excerpt":"by looking at the (easily available) data on the world’s static holdings of formal FX reserve assets, scholars and analysts miss most of the growth","claim":"Counting sovereign and quasi-sovereign foreign assets, rather than only formal reserves, changes the conclusion about where the official sector's dollar demand comes from.","role":"scope_choice","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[13,42],"reason":"Measuring only what is easy to observe can miss where the growth is happening."},{"excerpt":"given that FX reserve managers are themselves ultimately liability matchers","claim":"Reserve managers' currency choices largely mirror the currency of liabilities they must match, so the deeper drivers of dollar demand lie in the portfolio choices of other investors.","role":"stated_assumption","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[42],"reason":"Holders who match liabilities follow currency demand set elsewhere rather than creating it."},{"excerpt":"Most of the current flow into U.S. from the “official” sector is coming from investors who are not classic reserve managers.","claim":"Assets held by state-directed banks, pension funds and insurers can be treated as effectively sovereign even though they are legally separate from the central bank.","role":"hidden_assumption","explicit":false,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[7,32,33,43],"reason":"Treating assets as official requires that state control or backing outweighs legal separateness."},{"excerpt":"Adam Tooze has noted that inflows into the U.S. are now coming from investors looking for a profit, not investors looking for safety.","claim":"Tooze's 'profit dollar' idea, with inflows going to equities and corporate bonds rather than Treasuries, also describes sovereign and quasi-sovereign investors.","role":"evidence_source","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[39,40],"reason":"Return-seeking investors allocate toward risk assets, unlike safety-seeking reserve managers."},{"excerpt":"Put differently, the dollar’s global role is increasingly as a source of returns, not a source of safety. The foreign bid, private and public, is for risk, not for Treasuries.","claim":"Because the new official investors seek returns, foreign demand goes to U.S. risk assets rather than Treasuries, which keeps equity valuations extended without much helping Treasury financing.","role":"mechanism","explicit":true,"kind":"economic","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[46,39],"reason":"A shift in investor mandates from liquidity to return changes which assets receive inflows."},{"excerpt":"But the shift in the global investor base, and their apparent portfolio preference for U.S. risk assets in lieu of Treasuries, may help explain the divergence between the convenience yield on UST and the convenience yield on USD.","claim":"The shift in the investor base helps explain why the Treasury convenience yield has faded while the dollar keeps its privilege.","role":"intermediate_claim","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[47],"reason":"Demand for a currency can stay strong while demand for one instrument in it weakens."},{"excerpt":"That apparent premium on U.S. risk assets deserves as much (or more) scrutiny as the currency composition of central bank FX reserves.","claim":"Analysts should scrutinize the apparent premium on U.S. risk assets, the 'profit dollar', rather than obsessing over the reserve share.","role":"recommendation","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[41,48,46],"reason":"Attention should go to the asset prices most exposed to a shift in investor preferences."},{"excerpt":"And any real de-dollarization would likely occur first among these investors.","claim":"Real de-dollarization, if it comes, would show up first among quasi-sovereign investors rather than in reserves.","role":"intermediate_claim","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[45],"reason":"Change shows up first among the marginal, active buyers, not among static holders."}]}
